case_studies.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes. The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery. Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.
case_studies.summary: Large‑language‑model (LLM) servers can suffer a long‑lasting slowdown after a brief traffic spike, because the cache used to reuse conversation prefixes collapses and the system keeps working on stale requests. The authors built a tool called Basin that prioritises sessions, pre‑allocates cache for expected peak sizes, and drops excess load, restoring high throughput quickly. On real hardware Basin improved goodput by up to 3.6× compared with earlier cache‑first approaches.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference servers, check whether your cache policy can collapse after a spike: 1) monitor cache hit rates during short surges, 2) enable a priority‑based admission controller like Basin to reserve peak context sizes, 3) consider shedding low‑priority sessions when cache utilisation exceeds a threshold.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses cache instability in LLM agent serving, directly impacting infrastructure engineering for large language models. It presents a working system (Basin) with released code and real deployments, indicating high maturity. The solution offers actionable performance gains that could be packaged as a commercial service or integrated into existing AI infrastructure within a short timeframe, warranting a monetisation score of 15. Overall, the work scores well across all criteria.

case_studies.title: Ask, Don't Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents for Deep Kernel Optimization
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons. We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself. On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50x FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13x. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16x FlashAttention-3 and 1.46x FlashAttention-4 (geometric mean). Across 162 human messages and 11.5K agent tool calls, every large gain followed a question that moved the agent to a different layer of the system or rejected a claimed limit, never one that supplied information. We release the kernels, harness, question bank, and all traces.
case_studies.summary: KernelSeek is a question‑driven coding agent that improves CUDA kernels without needing expert knowledge, achieving up to 1.46x speedups on FlashAttention workloads. It uses short, well‑timed questions to steer optimisation, outperforming traditional scripted or open‑ended agents. This is relevant to cloud infrastructure teams that run GPU‑based workloads, offering a way to auto‑optimise kernels for better utilisation of GPU resources.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage GPU workloads, use KernelSeek by: 1) feeding it your current CUDA kernel and target performance goal; 2) allowing it to ask a few clarifying questions during optimisation; 3) reviewing the produced single‑file kernels that run without external libraries, then deploying them in your GPU clusters.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a question-driven LLM agent that optimizes CUDA kernels. While it introduces novel methods and provides open-source artifacts, the direct applicability to typical IT infrastructure tasks (SSO, endpoint management, cloud ops) is minimal. The system is experimentally validated and released, indicating a mature prototype, but practical deployment and commercial use within 90 days would be limited to niche GPU optimisation scenarios. Therefore, overall scores are low.

case_studies.title: Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR
case_studies.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can enable generalizable improvement for large language model (LLM) reasoning. This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies. We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x for equations f(x)=y, where f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g., more solutions, longer y, etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking, since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/ziqipang/rl_meta_thinking.
case_studies.summary: This study shows that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can teach large language models to use step‑by‑step reasoning, but fails when faced with new, harder problems. The researchers solved the problem by training the model on additional bijective tasks, which kept the correct reasoning strategy active even on out‑of‑distribution tests. As a result, the model’s accuracy under harder conditions improved significantly.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a reinforcement learning framework for improving LLM reasoning strategies. While it includes code and has practical implications for training LLMs, it does not directly impact day‑to‑day IT infrastructure operations, cloud or SaaS tooling, or immediate deployment for IT engineers. The concepts could influence future AI tooling but are not actionable within 90 days for UK IT engineers or consultants.

case_studies.title: Towards a Trustworthy and Governable Internet of Agentics: An Architectural Perspective on Protocols, Systems, and Services
case_studies.abstract: Large language model applications are increasingly being organized as tool-using and multi-agent workflows rather than as isolated chat interfaces. This perspective paper examines the architectural problem that follows from that shift: agents may reason, invoke tools, and delegate work, but dependable deployment still requires interoperability across frameworks, runtimes, data boundaries, and organizational control domains. We study this problem through the lens of the \emph{Internet of Agentics} (IoA), an emerging service-computing view in which heterogeneous agents are treated as governable service participants rather than only as stand-alone model endpoints. The paper organizes the landscape as a three-layer progression: from today's fragmented agent ecosystem, to interoperable agents, and ultimately to trustworthy and governable autonomy. First, it examines the protocol stack centered on the Agentic AI Foundation, including MCP for agent--tool interaction; A2A for agent--agent coordination; AGENTS.md and Skills-style procedural manifests; and discovery, transport, and trust mechanisms such as AGNTCY and SLIM. Second, it reviews the systems abstractions that make agents deployable as service components, including logical agent architectures, orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops, and hardware-aware inference infrastructure. Third, it situates these developments within services computing, arguing that agentic systems reinterpret classical concerns from SOA and microservices---discovery, composition, governance, pricing, and trust---at the level of cognitive capabilities rather than deterministic functions.
case_studies.summary: The paper proposes a new framework called the Internet of Agentics (IoA) to make large language model agents interoperable, governable, and trustworthy across different systems. It introduces a protocol stack (MCP, A2A, AGENTS.md, etc.) and system abstractions (orchestration, gateways, registries) to treat agents as service components. The result is a clearer pathway for deploying multi‑agent workflows in a controlled, secure, and scalable way.
case_studies.it_breakdown:
If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do:
1. Evaluate your current agent deployments against the IoA protocol stack (MCP for tool calls, A2A for agent‑to‑agent coordination).
2. Implement or adopt gateways and registries that expose agent services, enabling discovery and orchestration across your cloud environment.
3. Set up governance and trust layers (e.g., AGNTCY, SLIM) to monitor agent interactions and enforce organisational policies.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Perspective paper outlines architectural concepts for agent interoperability; provides useful high-level ideas for infrastructure but lacks concrete implementations or code. Real-world impact moderate but not immediate. AI maturity low because no deployed system. Monetisation potential low, no actionable service offering yet.

case_studies.title: A Living Leaderboard for Graph Machine Learning
case_studies.abstract: Graph machine learning benchmarking results are scattered across papers that use quite different sets of datasets and baseline methods, making it difficult to tell whether a reported gain reflects architectural progress or merely an outdated comparison or weakly tuned baseline. We introduce a living, graph-learning-specific leaderboard that organizes reported results by dataset, putting new results into context. As of 15 October 2026 our LLM-based extraction pipeline extracted 27,723 eligible results across 111 datasets from 885 peer-reviewed papers. Our analysis of these results quantifies concerns about graph-learning benchmarking: legacy datasets are still actively used and many result tables contain baseline results that are drastically lower than those already available in the literature, e.g. 45% Amazon-ratings tables and 37% for Peptides-struct. The leaderboard allows to quickly compare new results against compatible prior results, aiming to improve the overall quality of graph learning benchmarking.
case_studies.summary: The research tackles the chaos of scattered graph‑ML benchmarks by building a live, LLM‑powered leaderboard that gathers 27,723 results from 111 datasets and highlights outdated baselines. It shows many papers still use weak, legacy datasets, revealing gaps in current practice. For cloud infrastructure managers, it offers no direct operational benefit.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a living leaderboard for graph machine learning results. While it provides a useful resource for researchers and could aid in benchmarking, it does not directly influence day‑to‑day operations for IT engineers managing infrastructure or cloud services. The system is demonstrated and contains code, but it is still a research prototype rather than a production deployment, so maturity is moderate. The monetisation potential is low because the tool would need significant adaptation for commercial use and offers limited immediate value to an IT engineer or consultant within a 90‑day window. Overall, impact, maturity, and monetisation are modest, yielding a total score of 20.
